title: Languages & Scripts
description: Languages and scripts, taught in English as a bridge to Marathi, Sanskrit and the wider world: greetings in many languages, Marathi family, number, colour and animal words, Sanskrit numbers and words, writing systems of the world, the Devanagari script, language families, India's languages, Panini's Sanskrit grammar, words that travel between languages, linguistics, and language, identity and endangered languages. Marathi and Sanskrit words are shown with English pronunciation guides.

lessons.title: Many Ways to Say Hello
objectives: Say hello in at least four languages
Know that people around the world speak many languages
explanation: People around the world speak thousands of different languages — more than 7,000! Each language has its own way of saying hello.

In Marathi, we say "Namaskar" (nuh-muss-kaar). In Hindi and Sanskrit, "Namaste" (nuh-muss-tay). In Spanish, "Hola" (oh-la). In French, "Bonjour" (bon-zhoor). In Mandarin Chinese, "Nǐ hǎo" (nee how). In Japanese, "Konnichiwa".
Polite words matter in every language. In Marathi, thank you can be "Dhanyavaad" (dhun-ya-vaad), the same word used in Hindi.

vocabulary.meaning: the words people use to talk

examples: Saying "Namaskar" to Aaji with folded hands.

story.title: The Hello Train
story.text: Ivaan pretended to drive a train around the world. At the first stop, a teddy waved: "Namaskar!" At the next: "Bonjour!" Then: "Hola!" Then: "Konnichiwa!" At the last stop, Aaji was waiting with a smile. "Namaskar, Ivaan!" she said, folding her hands. Ivaan folded his hands too. "Namaskar, Aaji! I said hello all around the world!"

lessons.title: Aai, Baba and Everyone
objectives: Say Marathi words for family members

explanation: In Marathi, mother is "Aai" (aa-ee) and father is "Baba" (baa-baa).
Grandmother is "Aaji" (aa-jee) and grandfather is "Ajoba" (uh-jo-baa). An elder brother is often called "Dada" (daa-daa) and an elder sister "Tai" (taa-ee).
Families in different places use different words. In Hindi, mother is often "Maa" and grandmother "Dadi" or "Nani". Knowing family words helps us talk lovingly with our families.

lessons.title: Ek, Don, Teen
objectives: Count from 1 to 5 in Marathi
Count from 1 to 5 in Sanskrit
explanation: In Marathi, we count: 1 "ek", 2 "don", 3 "teen", 4 "chaar", 5 "paach".
In Sanskrit, an ancient language of India: 1 "ekam", 2 "dve", 3 "trini", 4 "chatvari", 5 "pancha".

Notice how similar some words are! Sanskrit is an ancient relative of Marathi and Hindi. Even English is distantly related: Sanskrit "trini" and English "three" both come from a very old shared ancestor language.
examples: Counting stairs: ek, don, teen, chaar, paach!

story.title: The Staircase Count
story.text: Every evening, Ivaan and Ajoba climbed the stairs together, counting in Marathi: "Ek, don, teen, chaar, paach!" One day Ajoba said, "Let's try Sanskrit." "Ekam, dve, trini, chatvari, pancha!" Ivaan giggled. "Pancha sounds like paach!" "Clever boy," said Ajoba. "They're cousins."

lessons.title: Letters, Syllables and Symbols
objectives: Describe different types of writing systems
Identify scripts used for different languages
explanation: A script is a system of writing. An alphabet, like the Latin alphabet used for English, has separate letters for consonants and vowels.

An abugida, like Devanagari (used for Marathi, Hindi, Sanskrit and Nepali), writes each consonant with a built-in "a" sound; other vowels are shown with marks added to the consonant. Many Indian scripts — Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Gujarati — are abugidas descended from the ancient Brahmi script.
Chinese uses logograms — characters that represent words or meaningful parts of words. Arabic and Urdu are written from right to left.

vocabulary.meaning: a set of letters for consonants and vowels
a script where consonants carry a built-in vowel
a character representing a word or meaning

story.title: The Mountain Picture
story.text: Zuri's teacher drew three peaks: 山. "This is the Chinese character for mountain," she said. "It started long ago as a picture." Then she wrote "मराठी" on the board. "This is Marathi in Devanagari — the line on top joins the letters." Zuri traced both in the air. "Every script is like a secret code!"

lessons.title: अ आ इ — Learning Devanagari
objectives: Recognise some Devanagari vowels and consonants
Explain how vowel marks (matras) change sounds
explanation: Devanagari letters hang from a line on top called the shirorekha. Vowels are called swar: अ (a), आ (aa), इ (i), ई (ee), उ (u), ऊ (oo).
Consonants are called vyanjan: क (ka), ख (kha), ग (ga), म (ma), न (na), र (ra). Each has a built-in "a" sound.

To change the vowel, add a mark called a matra: क (ka) + ा = का (kaa); क + ि = कि (ki). Devanagari letters are arranged scientifically by where in the mouth they are pronounced — from the throat to the lips.

vocabulary.meaning: a vowel mark added to a consonant
the line on top of Devanagari letters

story.title: Writing Aai

lessons.title: Family Trees of Languages
objectives: Describe major language families
Use word comparisons to show relationships
prerequisites: Knows similar number words in different languages
explanation: Like people, languages have families. Languages descended from a common ancestor share words and grammar patterns.

The Indo-European family includes Sanskrit, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Persian, Greek, Latin, English and German. Compare "mother": Sanskrit "mātṛ", Latin "mater", English "mother". In 1786, William Jones, a judge in Calcutta, noted Sanskrit's striking similarity to Greek and Latin.

The Dravidian family, mainly in South India, includes Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. India also has Austroasiatic languages (such as Santali and Khasi) and Tibeto-Burman languages (such as Manipuri/Meitei and Bodo).

vocabulary.meaning: languages descended from a common ancestor
a family including Sanskrit, Marathi and English
a family including Tamil and Telugu
words in related languages with a shared origin

examples: Tamil, one of the world's oldest living literary languages.

story.title: The Judge Who Noticed
story.text: In 1786, Sir William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta who studied Sanskrit, gave a famous lecture. He said Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were so alike that they must have "sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists." His idea helped start the scientific study of language families.

lessons.title: Unity in Many Languages
objectives: Explain India's linguistic diversity and constitutional recognition
Describe classical languages, including Marathi
explanation: India is one of the world's most linguistically diverse countries. The 2011 Census recorded 121 languages spoken by 10,000 or more people, and many more mother tongues.

The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 scheduled languages, including Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Sanskrit, Urdu, Kannada, Gujarati and Konkani. Hindi in Devanagari is the official language of the Union, with English also used for official purposes.

The government recognises some languages as "classical" for their antiquity and rich literature. In October 2024, Marathi received classical language status, along with Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali, joining Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Odia.

lessons.title: Panini and the Rules of Sanskrit
objectives: Describe Panini's contribution to linguistics
Explain and apply simple sandhi rules
explanation: Panini, a grammarian from Gandhara in north-west ancient India, composed the Ashtadhyayi ("eight chapters"), commonly dated to around the 4th century BCE. In about 4,000 compact rules (sutras), it describes Sanskrit's sounds and word formation with remarkable precision. Modern linguists and computer scientists admire its rule-based system.

Sandhi ("joining") describes how sounds change when words meet. For example, "deva" + "indra" becomes "devendra" (a + i → e), and "sūrya" + "udaya" becomes "sūryodaya", sunrise (a + u → o). Marathi words like "suryoday" show this too.
A simple Sanskrit sentence: "Bālakaḥ paṭhati" — "The boy reads." "Rāmaḥ vanam gacchati" — "Rama goes to the forest." Endings show who does what, so word order is flexible.

vocabulary.meaning: changing word endings to show grammar

story.title: A Grammar Like a Computer Program
story.text: In the 20th century, linguists studying Panini's Ashtadhyayi were amazed. Its rules called other rules, had priorities when they conflicted and used special markers — much like a computer program. Written over 2,000 years before computers, it remains one of the most complete grammars of any language ever made.

lessons.title: Shampoo, Jungle and Yoga
objectives: Identify loanwords between Indian languages and English
Explain how trade, rule and culture spread words
explanation: Languages borrow words. English took "yoga", "karma", "guru", "avatar", "mantra" and "nirvana" from Sanskrit and Pali.

Through trade and colonial contact, English borrowed from Hindi, Urdu, Marathi and other Indian languages: "shampoo" (from "chāmpo", to press), "bungalow" (from Bengali "bangla"), "jungle" (from "jangal"), "pyjama" (from Persian via Urdu) and "thug".

Marathi itself borrowed many words: from Persian and Arabic during Sultanate and Mughal times ("kagad", paper; "darwaja", door), and from Portuguese ("pav", bread; "batata", potato; "chavi", key). Borrowed words tell the story of history.

vocabulary.meaning: a word borrowed from another language

examples: Marathi "pav" (as in vada pav) from Portuguese "pão".

lessons.title: How Language Works
objectives: Describe the main branches of linguistics
Use the IPA and analyse word structure
explanation: Linguistics is the scientific study of language. Phonetics studies speech sounds; the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) gives one symbol per sound so any language can be written accurately. Marathi has retroflex sounds like ळ (ḷ), made by curling the tongue back.
Morphology studies how words are built from morphemes — the smallest meaningful units. "Unhappiness" = un + happy + ness. Marathi and Sanskrit use rich endings (inflection) to show case and tense.

Syntax studies sentence structure. English is usually Subject–Verb–Object ("Ivaan reads a book"), while Marathi is usually Subject–Object–Verb ("Ivaan pustak vachto" — Ivaan book reads). Noam Chomsky proposed that humans share an innate capacity for language — a theory still debated.

vocabulary.meaning: the smallest meaningful unit of language

story.title: The Retroflex Sound
story.text: A linguistics student from Spain struggled with the Marathi sound "ḷ" in "doḷa" (eye). Her Marathi friend showed her: curl your tongue back, touch the roof of your mouth, then say "l". She tried it ten times, laughing. Finally it came out right. "Your language has sounds I didn't know existed," she said. That's phonetics in action.

lessons.title: Saving Languages
objectives: Analyse the links between language, identity and power
Evaluate efforts to document and revive endangered languages
explanation: Language is closely tied to identity, culture and memory. In India, the 1950s–60s saw states reorganised along linguistic lines; Maharashtra was formed in 1960 after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement. Debates over which languages are used in schools, courts and government reflect questions of power and opportunity.

UNESCO estimates that around 40% of the world's languages are endangered — many with few remaining speakers, often because younger generations shift to dominant languages. When a language disappears, unique knowledge of plants, history and ways of thinking may be lost.

Revival efforts include documentation (recordings, dictionaries), teaching children, and media in the language. Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late 19th and 20th centuries; in India, projects document tribal languages, and the People's Linguistic Survey of India (led by G. N. Devy) recorded 780 languages.

vocabulary.meaning: a language at risk of no longer being spoken
a community moving to another language
recording a language for the future

examples: Recording elders telling stories in a tribal language.

story.title: The Last Speakers
story.text: A linguist visited a village where only a few elderly people still spoke their ancestral language fluently. Their grandchildren spoke the regional language instead. Together, the elders and the linguist recorded songs, stories and names of medicinal plants. The children helped make a picture dictionary — and began learning words their grandparents had feared would vanish.
